The Half Hitch Destin fishing blog's most recent accessible reports (dated late June 2026, roughly 4–6 weeks ago) are somewhat dated but consistent with the pattern: inshore action on trout and reds has been best early mornings and near dark on the flats, with menhaden used as live bait being a reliable producer around bayou mouths and docklines.

aiSummary: Choctawhatchee Bay is firing on speckled trout and redfish right now, with solid numbers of trout scattered across the bay and bull reds actively cruising — including a documented 40-plus-inch, 26-pound fish logged this past week. Water is 85°F and slightly stained under mostly cloudy skies, conditions that favor early aggression before a 50% storm chance arrives ahead of 4 PM. Get lines in the water at first light, fish hard through the high tide, and have a plan to get off exposed water well before early afternoon.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel where bait gets pushed through on both tides. Pilings hold speckled trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum year-round, with the lee-side pilings serving as the prime ambush zone on incoming tides. Open water at the bridge is exposed to wind and weather — it's typically the first spot on the bay to become unfishable when conditions build.
bridge.todaysCall: High tide crests around 8:15 AM, which is your best window here — bait will be funneling hard through the pilings right at first light on an incoming push that aligns almost perfectly with sunrise at 6:01 AM. The waning gibbous moon's spring-tide influence will strengthen that current flow, so work the lee-side pilings with live or cut bait during that morning push. WSW winds at 5–15 mph will create chop on the open span, but manageable early; with a 50% storm chance before 4 PM, plan to be off this exposed water by late morning. The slightly stained water and overcast sky actually favor the bridge bite — fish won't be as spooky in the shadow of the structure. Don't push your luck past noon given the storm window.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, plus speckled trout and flounder at the mouth. The oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime focal point, and tree cover keeps the bayou a few degrees cooler than the open bay while providing meaningful shelter from wind and weather. Upper reaches transition toward brackish water and can hold bass alongside smaller redfish.
alaqua.todaysCall: Tree cover and protected geometry make Alaqua a smart call today given WSW winds running 5–15 mph and a 50% storm chance before 4 PM — you can fish later into the morning here than on exposed water. Target the oyster bars at the creek mouth on the falling tide that begins after the 8:15 AM high, which will concentrate bait and hold redfish in ambush positions along the bar edges. The waning gibbous spring tide will produce a meaningful tidal drop through the afternoon, keeping current moving through the mouth well into midday. With water at 85°F and skies overcast, reds should stay active longer than usual — but still prioritize the early bite. Live bait worked along the oyster structure fits exactly the pattern producing across the bay right now.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees less fishing pressure than Alaqua and LaGrange, which tends to mean less-educated fish and a more willing bite. Interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for redfish in under two feet of water, and pompano occasionally appear at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer. Basin is less protected than LaGrange when weather builds, so it's better suited to calm or moderate conditions.
basin.todaysCall: Basin's interior grass flats are worth a look this morning on the tail end of the incoming tide and the early falling water after the 8:15 AM high — sight fishing for reds in skinny water is most productive with moving water and low light, both of which you'll have. Slightly stained water and heavy cloud cover will help you get closer to fish on the flats without spooking them. WSW winds at 5–15 mph are manageable here but watch how the afternoon develops — Basin is less sheltered than LaGrange if the storm chance materializes before 4 PM. The bay-wide bull red pattern is worth keeping in mind; work the mouth and any deeper edge adjacent to the grass as well. Be off the water or tucked into a protected corner well before early afternoon given the storm risk.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is the top trout producer among the spots covered in this report, anchored by legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deeper holes inside the bayou hold black drum and sheepshead, and the surrounding geography makes it the most protected water on this side of the bay. When weather builds and other spots become unmanageable, LaGrange is the default go-to.
lagrange.todaysCall: This is your safest high-percentage call today — protected water, top trout-and-red habitat, and the best weather margin of any open-bay-adjacent spot on the Freeport side. Fish the oyster bars at the mouth hard on the falling tide beginning after the 8:15 AM high; the strong spring-tide outflow from the waning gibbous moon will push bait off the flats and concentrate trout and reds along the bar edges. The bay-wide report confirms speckled trout are biting well with quality fish in the mix — this mouth is exactly the kind of structure that's been producing. If the storm threat accelerates, move deeper into the bayou toward the grass flats and interior holes where black drum and sheepshead hold. You can fish LaGrange comfortably well into late morning and make a clean exit before the pre-4 PM storm window tightens.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, with tidal flow pushing baitfish up the creek on incoming tides and concentrating redfish and trout in the bends and grass edges. The creek mouth is a recognized flounder zone, and upper sections transition toward brackish water where bass join smaller reds. Short and well-protected, it's the safest fishery on this part of the bay when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: Four Mile Creek is arguably the most weather-resilient option on the dashboard today — short, contained, and protected from the WSW wind that will be running 5–15 mph through the morning. The high tide at 8:15 AM marks the turnaround; get in position early while bait is still being pushed up the creek, then fish the falling water through the bends and grass edges as reds and trout set up in ambush positions. The creek mouth is worth a few casts for flounder on the drop, especially with slightly stained water that keeps them less wary of a leader. With a 50% storm chance before 4 PM, this is one of the few spots where you can fish confidently through midday without an aggressive exit plan. Keep presentations tight to structure — current bends and undercut grass edges are your targets on the outgoing tide.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide spot and one of the most consistently productive trout flats on Choctawhatchee Bay. Summer mornings are peak season here, with trout stacking on grass in two to four feet of water, and Spanish mackerel show at the mouth on moving tides. It sees regular pressure but produces reliably — note that it's further from the 331 Bridge than the other bayous, so factor run time into your planning.
hogtown.todaysCall: If you're making the run to Hogtown, leave early — sunrise is 6:01 AM and summer mornings on these grass flats are the money window before heat and boat traffic build. Trout should be stacked in 2–4 feet on the flats with overcast skies and slightly stained water giving you favorable low-light conditions through the morning; this matches the bay-wide pattern of quality speckled trout biting right now. The high tide at 8:15 AM means you'll arrive with water on the grass and a falling tide incoming shortly after — a prime setup for working the flat edges with soft plastics or live bait. Spanish mackerel are a possibility at the mouth on the moving water; keep a faster presentation ready if you see surface activity. The longer run means you need to be watching the western sky closely — give yourself a firm turnaround time of no later than late morning given the storm window before 4 PM.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary that feeds directly into LaGrange Bayou, just south of Freeport. Its direct connection to LaGrange — this dashboard's top trout producer — means the same oyster-bar trout-and-redfish pattern plausibly extends into this quieter, less-pressured water, though documented fishing history for Mallet itself is limited. Small and interior, it functions well as a calm-water fallback when wind makes the open bay uncomfortable.
mallet.todaysCall: Mallet's value today is its combination of protection and proximity to LaGrange's proven bite — if the LaGrange mouth is crowded or you want to explore quieter water in the same neighborhood, Mallet is a logical extension of the same trip. WSW winds at 5–15 mph and a pre-4 PM storm chance both favor interior, sheltered water, which Mallet provides. Fish it the same way you'd approach LaGrange: work any oyster or hard-bottom structure near the confluence on the falling tide after the 8:15 AM high. Expect reds and trout to be the realistic targets given the species overlap with its larger neighbor. Documented catch data here is thin, so treat it as a bonus exploratory stop rather than a primary destination.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — a long-run destination rather than a quick local trip. It shares the protected-bayou character of Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, and a few interior holes, and sees lighter pressure largely because of the distance involved. It neighbors Hewett Bayou and Buck Bayou immediately to the east, making all three realistically fishable on the same run.
mack.todaysCall: The long run to Mack Bayou is the primary consideration today — with a 50% storm chance before 4 PM, you need to be confident in your weather read before committing to a distant destination with a long return trip. If conditions look stable at first light and you have reliable weather monitoring, the light pressure and protected habitat here are genuine draws. Target oyster bars and marsh grass edges on the falling tide that develops after the 8:15 AM high; the spring-tide outflow will be meaningful and should concentrate fish along structure. Pair this with Hewett and Buck Bayou to maximize the run; reds and trout are the realistic targets based on both habitat and the bay-wide bite pattern. Build in a firm departure time — you do not want to be running back across open bay water when afternoon storms fire.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. It shares the same protected-bayou habitat as its neighbors — oyster bars and marsh grass at the mouth, deeper interior holes further in — and sees light pressure due to its distance from the main boat ramps. It pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou as part of the same long-run trip.
hewett.todaysCall: Same weather calculus applies here as Mack Bayou — the long run from the 331 Bridge means today's storm risk before 4 PM needs to be evaluated honestly before you leave the ramp. If you make the run, fish Hewett's mouth structure on the falling tide after the 8:15 AM high, working oyster bars and marsh grass edges where bait will be moving out with the strong spring-tide drop. Slightly stained water and overcast skies should keep redfish and trout less wary and feeding longer into the morning. Hewett is naturally bundled with Mack and Buck — plan a logical drift sequence through all three to cover water efficiently. Hard departure by late morning is non-negotiable given the storm window and run time back.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should track its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there is less basis to speak confidently about its productivity. It's best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a standalone destination worth a dedicated run.
buck.todaysCall: Buck Bayou makes sense only as a quick bonus stop folded into a Mack and Hewett trip — the run time and today's storm risk before 4 PM make it hard to justify as a standalone destination. If you're already in the neighborhood, fish any visible oyster or grass-edge structure on the falling tide after the 8:15 AM high with the same approach you'd use at Hewett. Expect redfish and trout given the habitat type, but documented catch history here is thin so keep expectations calibrated. The limited size means you can cover the fishable water quickly and move on without sacrificing much time. Weather urgency is the same as its neighbors — be running back before the storm window tightens mid-morning.
